KEY MESSAGE 1...Cooler and dry through Wednesday as high 
pressure builds.

Broad high pressure begins to build over the Great Lakes and 
push east into New England today, then moving northeast through 
Atlantic Canada Wednesday. Expecting this high to strengthen 
upwards of 1040mb as it progresses across New England, allowing 
850mb temperatures to drop from near 0C currently to -6C by this
evening. 925mb temperatures are also expected to drop 
throughout today from just above freezing to near -4C and hover 
there through Wednesday. This will support afternoon high 
temperatures in the 40s both today and Wednesday. The cooler 
temperatures will be most noticeable tonight and Wednesday night
as (mostly) clear skies and calmer winds will help support 
radiational cooling...overnight lows tonight likely drop into 
the upper teens for the higher elevations and low 20s for most 
others. However, the Cape, Islands, and immediate coastal 
communities may see those temperatures hovering right around 
freezing. Slightly warmer low temperatures expected for 
Wednesday night with an increasing cloud deck ahead of the 
upcoming storm.... likely in the low 20s for the higher 
elevations and upper 20s elsewhere (upper 30s for the Cape, 
Islands, and immediate Coast).

KEY MESSAGE 2...Confidence remains high in a coastal storm 
Thanksgiving Day into Friday, with dangerous marine conditions, 
potential coastal flooding and beach erosion, strong winds, and 
periods of heavy rainfall.

There hasn't been much deviation in the longer-range guidance, 
which continues to indicate an impactful coastal storm 
Thanksgiving Day into Friday. However, there is a glimmer of 
hope for a drier start to Thanksgiving, with the onset of rain 
perhaps holding off until late morning. This will also coincide 
with increasing southeasterly winds. As previous forecasters 
have mentioned, our primary concerns with this coastal storm are
dangerous marine conditions, potential coastal flooding, 
particularly if the strongest winds align with the higher 
astronomical tides, beach erosion, strong wind gusts, and 
urban/poor drainage flooding due to localized heavy downpours. 
It is worth noting that refinements to the forecast are likely 
over the next couple of days, as this system has yet to develop.
In fact, the coastal low isn't expected to develop for another 
24 hours or so. As previously discussed, development occurs off 
the coast of Florida, with the associated southern stream 
shortwave eventually being absorbed by a more potent northern 
stream shortwave. This allows for the advection of a moisture-
rich air mass into the Northeast. The highly amplified upper-
level flow associated with the vigorous northern stream energy 
favors a track farther west than that of a traditional 
nor'easter, as previous forecasters have noted. As the low 
pressure system lifts northward toward southern New England, a 
departing 1040+ mb high over New England and the Canadian 
Maritimes will result in the development of a tight pressure 
gradient as the low to our south deepens below 1000 mb. There is
moderate to high confidence in the general position of the low 
on Thursday, as global ensembles place it in the vicinity of the
Carolinas. However, confidence decreases heading into Friday, 
with ensemble solutions ranging from the Ohio River Valley to 
the Mid-Atlantic coast. Steering flow becomes west-northwesterly
late Friday night into early Saturday, allowing the system to 
exit toward the Canadian Maritimes.

Coastal & Marine Impacts: Astronomical tides are among the 
highest of the year heading into Thanksgiving, with Boston's 
midday high tide projected to reach 11.84 ft MLLW, while the 
overnight high tide is considerably lower at 9.89 ft MLLW. This 
is followed by another high tide of 11.67 ft MLLW around 1 PM 
Friday. As of this update, we continue to anticipate the 
strongest southeasterly winds arriving Thursday night into early
Friday morning, which would generally coincide with the lower 
of the three high tide cycles. While this is encouraging, a 
shift in the timing of the strongest winds by several hours in 
either direction could have significant implications for the 
magnitude of coastal flooding. Additionally, the farther west 
track would favor winds eventually becoming more southerly, 
limiting the duration of the strongest southeasterly winds. 
Given the prolonged period of southeast winds, significant wave 
action along the coast is likely, though uncertainty remains 
regarding the magnitude of storm surge associated with this 
system. It will take relatively little surge to produce coastal 
flooding impacts during either of the midday high tides. At 
Boston, less than a foot of storm surge would bring water levels
to 12.3 ft MLLW, where shallow pockets of flooding less than
